response.text:
Education, like politics, is a rough affair, and every instructor has to shut his eyes and hold his tongue as though he were a priest. The college had pleaded guilty, and tried to reform. He had pleaded guilty from the start, and his reforms had failed before those of the college.

The lecture-room was futile enough, but the faculty-room was worse. Several score of the best-educated, most agreeable, and personally the most sociable people in America united in Cambridge to make a social desert that would have starved a polar bear. The liveliest and most agreeable of men tried their best to break out and be like other men in Cambridge and Boston, but society called them professors, and professors they had to be. Society was a faculty-meeting without business.

Of all his many educations, Adams thought that of school-teacher the thinnest. Yet the education of an editor was thinner still — a helpless drudge whose successes belonged to his writers, whose failures might bankrupt himself, and whose chief secret of success was the getting of advertisements. A professor had at least the pleasure of associating with his students; an editor lived the life of an owl. On the whole, Adams preferred his attic in Washington. Ignorance paid better, for at least it earned fifty dollars a month.

With this result Henry Adams's education, at his entry into life, stopped, and his life began. The editorship of the *North American Review* had one solitary merit: it made the editor acquainted at a distance with almost every one in the country who could write. Among them, only one stood out as the type and model of what Adams would have liked to be, and of what the American, as he conceived, should have been and was not.

When his first year of professing and editing was over, he took the next train for the West. In 1871 the West was still fresh, and the Union Pacific was young. Beyond the Missouri one felt the atmosphere of Indians and buffaloes. The topographers and geologists of the Survey held under their hammers a thousand miles of mineral country with all its riddles to solve. They felt the future in their hands.

One morning, camped above Estes Park on the flank of Long's Peak, Adams borrowed a rod and rode down for trout. Darkness caught him before he could catch his trail. The patient mule plodded on until at last a light showed in the distance. As they came up to the cabin door, two or three men came out to see the stranger.

One of them was Clarence King, on his way up to the camp. Adams fell into his arms. As with most friendships, it was never a matter of growth or doubt. Friends are born in archaic horizons; they were shaped with the *Pteraspis* in Siluria; they have nothing to do with the accident of space. They shared the room and the bed, and talked till far towards dawn.

King had everything to interest and delight Adams. He knew more than Adams did of art and poetry; he knew America, especially west of the hundredth meridian, better than any one; he knew the professor by heart, and the Congressman better than the professor. He knew even women; even the American woman; even the New York woman, which is saying much. The charm of King was that he saw what others did and a great deal more. His wit and humor; his bubbling energy which swept every one into the current of his interest; his personal charm of youth and manners; his faculty of giving and taking, profusely, lavishly, whether in thought or in money as though he were Nature herself, marked him almost alone among Americans. He had in him something of the Greek — a touch of Alcibiades or Alexander. One Clarence King only existed in the world.

A new friend is always a miracle, but at thirty-three years old, such a bird of paradise rising in the sage-brush was an avatar. King, like Adams, was at that moment passing the critical point of his career. The one, coming from the west, saturated with the sunshine of the Sierras, met the other, drifting from the east, drenched in the fogs of London, and both had the same problems to handle — the same field to work in — the same obstacles to overcome.

King had moulded and directed his life logically, scientifically, as Adams thought American life should be directed. He could look back and look forward on a straight line, with scientific knowledge for its base. Adams's life, past or future, was a succession of violent breaks or waves, with no base at all. King's abnormal energy had already won him great success: he had induced Congress to adopt almost its first modern act of legislation, had organized a civil Government Survey, had paralleled the Continental Railway in Geology. Whatever prize he wanted lay ready for him — scientific, social, literary, political. With ordinary luck he would die at eighty the richest and most many-sided genius of his day.

So little egoistic he was that none of his friends felt envy of his superiority, but rather grovelled before it. The men worshipped not so much their friend as the ideal American they all wanted to be.

In camp far up in the Uintahs these talks were continued till the frosts became sharp in the mountains. To King and his men, catastrophe was the law of change; they cared little for simplicity and much for complexity. King loved paradox; he started them like rabbits, and cared for them no longer, when caught or lost; but they delighted Adams, for they helped to persuade him that history was more amusing than science.

No more education was possible for either man. When Adams started back to Cambridge, to take up again the humble tasks of schoolmaster and editor, he was harnessed to his cart. Education, systematic or accidental, had done its worst. Henceforth, he went on, submissive.
